namic collaborative ﬁltering. The model uses the matrix
factorization approach, which embeds users and objects in a
latent space. However, unlike most related models in which
these locations are ﬁxed in time, we allowed them to drift
according to a Brownian motion. This allows for dynamic
evolution of, e.g., user preference. We built on this basic
model by presenting a method for learning a time-evolving
drift parameter for the state space vectors using a geometric
Brownian motion.
Many other applications could potentially beneﬁt from
this framework. For example, we could predict results of bat-
ter/pitcher events over time in baseball or winners of sporting
competitions. Such a dynamic model would clearly be an
advantage since player or team performance can experience
streaks and slumps. Another potential use is in automated
tutoring systems, where a student is asked a sequence of
questions (e.g., math questions or language ﬂashcards). In
a collaborative ﬁltering environment we would wish to
estimate the probability that a student answers a question
correctly. Clearly as the student learns these probabilities
will evolve. Having estimates for such a probability would
allow for intelligent tutoring, where questions are selected

the learning process.","score":1.879683101959135,"position":0,"hidden_text":false,"source":"extracted","bbox":[54,346.3,297,644.8],"page_rect":[0,0,612,792],"clip":[0.088,0.437,0.485,0.814]},{"path":"/Users/jztan/src/pdf-mcp/benchmark_data/.reading_order_pdfs/1608.03983.pdf","doc_title":null,"page":3,"excerpt":"When optimizing multimodal functions one may want to ﬁnd all global and local optima. tractability of this task depends on the landscape of the function at hand and the budget of func-
tion evaluations. Gradient-free optimization approaches based on niching methods (Preuss, 2015)
usually can deal with this task by covering the search space with dynamically allocated niches of
local optimizers. However, these methods usually work only for relatively small search spaces,
e.g., n < 10, and do not scale up due to the curse of dimensionality (Preuss, 2010). Instead, the
current state-of-the-art gradient-free optimizers employ various restart mechanisms (Hansen, 2009;
Loshchilov et al., 2012). One way to deal with multimodal functions is to iteratively sample a large
number λ of candidate solutions, make a step towards better solutions and slowly shape the sampling
distribution to maximize the likelihood of successful steps to appear again (Hansen & Kern, 2004).
The larger the λ, the more global search is performed requiring more function evaluations. In order
to achieve good anytime performance, it is common to start with a small λ and increase it (e.g., by
doubling) after each restart. This approach works best on multimodal functions with a global funnel
structure and also improves the results on ill-conditioned problems where numerical issues might

We have presented a collaborative Kalman ﬁlter for dy-
namic collaborative ﬁltering. The model uses the matrix

drift parameter for the state space vectors using a geometric
Brownian motion.

this framework. For example, we could predict results of bat-
ter/pitcher events over time in baseball or winners of sporting
competitions. Such a dynamic model would clearly be an
advantage since player or team performance can experience
streaks and slumps. Another potential use is in automated
tutoring systems, where a student is asked a sequence of
questions (e.g., math questions or language ﬂashcards). In
a collaborative ﬁltering environment we would wish to
estimate the probability that a student answers a question
correctly. Clearly as the student learns these probabilities
will evolve. Having estimates for such a probability would
allow for intelligent tutoring, where questions are selected
that are not too easy or too hard and are able to help with
the learning process.

When optimizing multimodal functions one may want to ﬁnd all global and local optima. The
tractability of this task depends on the landscape of the function at hand and the budget of func-
tion evaluations. Gradient-free optimization approaches based on niching methods (Preuss, 2015)
usually can deal with this task by covering the search space with dynamically allocated niches of
local optimizers. However, these methods usually work only for relatively small search spaces,
e.g., n < 10, and do not scale up due to the curse of dimensionality (Preuss, 2010). Instead, the
current state-of-the-art gradient-free optimizers employ various restart mechanisms (Hansen, 2009;
Loshchilov et al., 2012). One way to deal with multimodal functions is to iteratively sample a large
number λ of candidate solutions, make a step towards better solutions and slowly shape the sampling
distribution to maximize the likelihood of successful steps to appear again (Hansen & Kern, 2004).

structure and also improves the results on ill-conditioned problems where numerical issues might

## "Stochastic dynamics" across the corpus

The corpus has no single paper titled "stochastic dynamics," but the concept is a working tool in several of the July-2026 (`2607.*`) preprints and a few older ones. Here is what each contributes, most central first.

### Papers where stochastic dynamics is a core modeling tool

**1. Collective learning in populations of adaptive agents — `2607.02171`**
This paper builds directly on the stochastic dynamics of individual active agents. The single-agent "physical dynamics" are the standard stochastic active-matter models: two-dimensional Active Brownian Particles (ABP), Run-and-Tumble Particles (RTP), and active Ornstein–Uhlenbeck particles (AOUP). For ABP the self-propulsion angle θ diffuses with angular diffusion coefficient D_R; for RTP θ performs *stochastic jumps* at rate λ_R to a new angle drawn from ψ(θ′|θ) (p. 3). On top of this positional stochasticity the authors add **Langevin noise in the memory dynamics** and use kinetic theory (borrowed from active matter) to derive a macroscopic evolution equation for the policy distribution (p. 2), explicitly drawing on concepts from stochastic thermodynamics (p. 1).

**2. Thermodynamics of Quantum Reservoir Computing — `2607.02157`**
This is a *stochastic thermodynamics* paper. It argues that continuously updating a quantum memory "inevitably incurs non-equilibrium thermodynamic costs, including stochastic work, heat dissipation, and information processing," and connects macroscopic predictive performance to "microscopic stochastic thermodynamics" (p. 3). Concretely, it applies stochastic thermodynamics to the *unraveled microscopic quantum trajectories*, tracking fluctuating work and heat at the single-trajectory level; the microscopic stochastic work w_{n+1} on the reservoir equals the energy differential of the driving field during an instantaneous quench (p. 5). Summing these fluctuating quantities recovers a macroscopic first law W_tot = ΔU_tot + Q_diss (p. 6), generalizing the Landauer bound (pp. 5–6, 26).

**3. Path-Measure Dynamics of Attention-Driven World Models — `2607.02154`**
Here the latent (hidden-state) dynamics are cast as a stochastic process viewed as a *measure over paths* (Onsager–Machlup / path-integral framing, per the title). Eliminating fast variables yields the observed dynamics as a **nonlocal generalized Langevin equation** — the memory kernel is generated by the elimination rather than assumed (p. 3). The memory kernel can be recovered empirically from latent trajectories z(t) and the learned drift by regularized deconvolution of that generalized Langevin equation, then tested for membership in the completely-monotone class (p. 6). Its reference list situates this in the score-based-SDE / diffusion-model literature (Song et al., "Score-Based Generative Modeling through Stochastic Differential Equations"; the Onsager–Machlup transition-path-sampling work) (p. 7).

**4. Learning the Brain's Dynamics as a Port-Hamiltonian System — `2607.10439`**
The model has an explicit stochastic component: a **Fluctuation–Dissipation-consistent noise channel produces stochastic trajectories** from the phasor state (p. 2). Run forward, this "stochastic free-run reproduces near-critical avalanche dynamics, with a branching parameter" near criticality (p. 18) — i.e. the stochastic dynamics recover the empirically-observed neuronal-avalanche statistics.

### Papers where stochastic dynamics appears in a more domain-specific / narrower sense

**5. Robustness in Sequential Decision Making — High-Frequency Market Making — `2607.08291`**
The state evolution is described as "only partially stochastic": part of the state evolves deterministically while other components depend on *random market innovations*, and the two are formally separated (deterministic subspace Ω_det vs. stochastic-innovation subspace Ω_rnd) (p. 9). Uncertainty about the future *transition dynamics* is then modeled with optimal-transport (Sinkhorn) ambiguity sets around a reference model (p. 9).

**6. Estimating the Stochastic Discount Factor from Option Prices — `2607.08500`**
"Stochastic" here is the finance-theoretic stochastic discount factor (SDF); the paper proposes an SDF scaled by time-varying volatility (p. 1). This is stochastic in the pricing-kernel sense rather than an explicit dynamical (SDE) model.

**7. Collaborative Kalman filter (dynamic collaborative filtering) — `1501.05624`**
Latent user/object embeddings are not fixed but "drift according to a Brownian motion," with a time-evolving drift parameter learned via a geometric Brownian motion (p. 10) — a stochastic-dynamics treatment of latent state.

**8. Population-genetics selection inference — `1606.06090`**
Works with single trajectories of a *stochastic process governed by selection and genetic drift*, using Brownian bridges and the Doob h-transform to condition trajectories on both initial and final states (p. 10).

### Incidental / false matches (mentioned for completeness)

These matched the two keywords but do **not** treat stochastic dynamics as a topic: `0710.2265` (cardiac-chaos control) only notes in passing that PPF control "can be used even in systems with stochastic dynamics" (p. 4); `1502.03167` (Batch Normalization) merely cites Saxe et al.'s "nonlinear dynamics of learning" (p. 9, reference list); `2607.09990` (Political Power in International Trade) matched only the journal name *Review of Economic Dynamics* (p. 63); `2607.02093` (integrable quantum circuits) uses "dynamical evolution operator" deterministically (p. 32); and `1608.03983` (SGDR) matched "stochastic"+"dynamically" incidentally (p. 3).

### Bottom line
If "stochastic dynamics" means an explicit stochastic-process model of how a system evolves, the strongest treatments in this corpus are the four `2607.*` physics/ML papers: agent-level active-matter Langevin/ABP/RTP/AOUP dynamics (`2607.02171`, p. 3), single-trajectory stochastic thermodynamics (`2607.02157`, pp. 3–6), path-measure / generalized-Langevin latent dynamics (`2607.02154`, pp. 3, 6), and fluctuation–dissipation-driven stochastic neural trajectories (`2607.10439`, pp. 2, 18). The finance and biology papers (`2607.08291` p. 9, `2607.08500` p. 1, `1501.05624` p. 10, `1606.06090` p. 10) apply the same idea in their own domains.
